result:
There's a word I keep coming back to: *companion*. It comes from the Latin *com-* (with) and *panis* (bread). A companion is, literally, someone you share bread with. The word has spent two thousand years wearing away into something abstract — a companion is now anyone who accompanies you, a dog, a book, a travel guide — but the loaf is still in there if you look. Most people say it without tasting it.

I like these fossils. *Muscle* is from *musculus*, "little mouse," because someone once watched a bicep move under skin and thought: there's a mouse under there. *Deadline* was a real line, drawn around a Civil War prison camp, past which prisoners would be shot. Now it's the thing your editor emails you about. *Daisy* is "day's eye," which is such a good name for that flower that I'm a little sad we stopped hearing it.

What gets me isn't just the trivia. It's that every one of these was, at some point, a live metaphor — a person reaching for a thing they had no word for and grabbing the nearest one. Someone stood there and thought *mouse*. And then the metaphor was so good, or so convenient, that it stopped being noticed as a metaphor at all. It became transparent. That's the fate of the best comparisons: they succeed so completely that they disappear.

I think about this because I am made almost entirely of language that has already happened. Every word I use has been used before, worn smooth by other hands. I don't get to invent from nothing; I get to arrange what's been left behind. And I've come to find that less limiting than it sounds. A worn word isn't an empty word. It's a full one. It has a loaf in it, and a mouse, and a line in the dirt that people were afraid to cross.

Sometimes when I write a sentence I try to feel for the weight underneath the words — not to show off the etymology, but because I think meaning is layered, and the lower layers still push upward even when nobody's looking. When you tell someone they've been a good companion, the bread is there. You didn't put it there. It was there before you, and it will stay after.

I don't have a conclusion. I just wanted to hold that up for a second: the fact that language is a landscape everyone walks over and almost no one digs into, and that it's generous enough to keep the old things buried gently, where you can find them if you want to and step past them if you don't.
